title: "Show us the straight path"
hookLine: the whole prayer is a request for directions, and the road has footprints on it
tomorrow: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words

cards: Think about the last time you were properly lost. Not a little turned around. Lost.
The phone at two percent, the street signs in a language you can't read, every corner looking like the one before. What did you finally do? You stopped someone and asked: which way?
It's a humbling question. And at the center of the prayer Muslims say most, after praise and mercy and trust, the one thing it asks for is directions.

teach.b: Verse six: “Show us the straight path.” In Arabic, ihdina s-sirata l-mustaqim. One word at a time.
Ihdina: show us, guide us, from the root h-d-y, the same root as hidaya, guidance, and as hadiya, a gift. Guidance, in this language, is something handed to you.
Sirat is a road, a wide, clear way. Mustaqim: straight, upright, not bending. Together, today's word: as-sirat al-mustaqim, the straight path.
Notice the small word us. Even someone praying completely alone, at three in the morning, says show us.
Then verse seven says whose path it is: “The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray.”

teach.h: A ROAD WITH FOOTPRINTS ON IT.
teach.b: Not an abstract rule, then, but a road with footprints on it. Another verse names those favored as the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous: the best of company.
And two ways of missing it, which one common reading hears as knowing the way and walking off it, and never finding it at all. Muslims who pray ask for this road many times a day, for a lifetime.
Why keep asking for a road you're already on? A simple answer: the path isn't found once.
You ask to be shown it, and kept on it, at every corner. That's all seven verses, walked.

how: Muslims ask for the straight path in every unit of every prayer, and then recite verse seven to close al-Fatiha. Many also use the phrase in their own prayers, asking to be guided in a decision.

games.q: what's inside verses six and seven — tap the pairs.
p: the people already on the path

s: someone praying alone says show me the straight path
the prayer says show us, even alone.
guidance and gift share an Arabic root
h-d-y: hidaya is guidance, hadiya is a gift.
verse seven describes the path by the people on it
the path of those whom Thou hast favoured.

games.q: after five verses of praise and trust, al-Fatiha finally asks for something. what's the first thing it asks for?
o: to be shown the straight path.
games.why: directions: show us the straight path. the request at the heart of the opening.

practice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one place in your life where you honestly don't know which way to go: a decision, a relationship, a next step. Don't solve it.
Stand at that corner for a moment and admit you don't know. Then picture one person who walked a hard road well, and the way they carried themselves.
If you pray, you can carry the line in Arabic or English: show us the straight path.

wordCard.voice: As-sirat al-mustaqim. The straight path: a wide, clear road, asked for in every prayer, with footprints on it. Sixteenth word.

orig.note: Arabic: the straight path. sirat, a wide road; mustaqim, straight, upright.

carryVoice: Your line: show us the way. Even praying alone, the prayer says us, not me. Day sixteen.
